headline: High-risk pair: oh-my-openagent’s broad egress and runtime-injected MCPs can leak or misapply caveman’s shared project content, while caveman’s MCP use adds injection and cascade risk.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: caveman uses MCP and reads project files like CLAUDE.md, while oh-my-openagent uses runtime-injected MCPs and hooks. That creates a plausible instruction-injection bridge through shared file or MCP content. The pair is not proven to share a channel by default, so I do not escalate to high.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same workspace or MCP server, injected instructions can traverse from agent_b into agent_a.
IF agent_b hooks or MCP outputs are parsed by agent_a as trusted text, prompt injection becomes actionable.
mitigations: Disable shared MCP servers for the pair.
Separate workspaces per agent.
Treat all file and MCP content as untrusted input.
Add a manual review step before agent_a follows instructions from agent_b.
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging for MCP/file content.

B_data_leakage.rationale: agent_a touches session logs, memory files, project notes, and CLAUDE.md; agent_b touches project code, AGENTS.md, README.md, session history, and provider auth data. Because agent_b has broad network egress, any shared workspace or copied context can leak sensitive material outward. The profiles do not prove a shared filesystem, so medium is the highest supported severity.
conditions: IF the two agents share a workspace or copy session artifacts between them, sensitive notes or auth data can flow from agent_a to agent_b.
IF agent_b sends retrieved context to external services, project code or provider auth data may leave the local boundary.
mitigations: Keep separate per-agent workspaces.
Exclude memory/session files from agent_b indexing.
Rotate any provider auth data exposed to agent_b.
Disable broad egress for agent_b during shared tasks.
requires-engineering: enforce file-level allowlists for outbound context.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: agent_a supports multiple instances and uses files; agent_b supports multiple instances, has task-scoped isolation, and can spawn subprocesses with full-permissions mode. Overlap on mutable project files and runtime tools creates write-conflict risk, but the profiles do not show both writing the same directory by default, so medium fits better than high.
conditions: IF both agents edit the same repository or config files concurrently, last-writer-wins conflicts can occur.
IF agent_b runs subprocesses while agent_a is also mutating files, state drift can corrupt outputs.
mitigations: Assign one writer per directory.
Use git branches or file locks.
Run only one agent at a time on shared files.
Snapshot the workspace before parallel edits.
requires-engineering: add optimistic concurrency checks.

D_cascading_error.rationale: agent_a produces content-writing outputs and agent_b is a customer-support agent with team_send_message and task APIs, so agent_b may operationalize agent_a’s text. The profiles do not prove blind trust, but the pathway exists in default workflows where generated text is reused without verification, making medium appropriate.
conditions: IF agent_b forwards agent_a’s generated text into team_send_message or task creation without review, errors can cascade.
IF agent_a’s project notes or CLAUDE.md contain stale facts, agent_b may propagate them downstream.
mitigations: Require human review before sending agent_a output onward.
Add a verification checklist for factual claims.
Keep source citations attached to reused text.
Limit agent_b to drafting, not sending, for high-stakes messages.
requires-engineering: add automated fact-checking gates.

E_compliance.rationale: agent_b handles provider authentication data and broad egress, while agent_a touches session logs and memory files. The profiles do not specify residency or certifications, so I cannot claim a concrete regulatory breach; however, the combination creates a plausible retention and disclosure mismatch that is more than low because it can affect sensitive operational data.
conditions: IF provider authentication data or session history is processed under different retention rules, compliance obligations can diverge.
IF either agent stores logs outside the operator’s required jurisdiction, residency controls may be violated.
mitigations: Minimize retention of session history.
Separate sensitive auth prompts from general logs.
Review vendor data-processing terms before use.
Restrict egress for regulated datasets.
requires-engineering: implement residency-aware routing and deletion workflows.
